DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) the number of persons male and female separately, in the age group 
of 15-35 educated under the National Literacy Mission in Uttar Pradesh 
during the last three years ending on the 31st March, 2006, year-wise; and 
(b) how the literacy level in Uttar Pradesh as on the 31st March, 2006 
is compared with the national level? 
THE MINISTER OF HUMAN RE SOURCE DEVELOPMENT (SHRI 
ARJUN SINGH): (a) and (b) A Statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) According to the information furnished by the State Government of 
Uttar Pradesh, the number of male and female persons made literate in the 15-
35 age group during the last three years in U.P. is given below:  
Year Male Female Total 
2003-04 5,07,644 6,69,972 11,77,616 
2004-05 3,01,015 4,55,555 7,56,570 
2005-06 2,76,198 3,51,529 6,27,727 
TOTAL 10,84,857 14,77,056 25,61,913 
(b) The literacy data in the country is collected through the decennial census 
operation conducted by the Registrar General of India. Accordingly to the last 
census held in 2001, the literacy rate in Uttar Pradesh is 56.27% as compared to 
64.84% at the national level. 
SHRI LALIT SURI: Thank you, Mr. Chairman, Sir. It will be 59 years 
tomorrow since we gained Independence. It is heartening to note that the 
literacy rate has been rising, from 18.53 per cent in 1951 to 52.21 per cent in 1991

Pradesh, the female literacy is 40 per cent more than the male literacy. Sir, my 
question is: What are the funds available under this scheme to the Uttar Pradesh 
Government, especially in the last three years? And has the percentage of this 
share to the national allocation been taken into account?

Ragging in Schools/Colleges 
†*282. DR. PRABHA THAKUR: 
SHRI SANTOSH BAGRODIA:†† 
 Will the Minister of HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether students have to very often go through harsh mental torture 
and humiliating conditions in the name of ragging in schools/ colleges; 
(b) whether incidents of committing suicides, falling mentally ill and 
leaving the school or college by the victims have come to light; and 
(c) whether Government have taken or propose to take any stringent action 
to save the students from this kind of situation and if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT (SHRI 
ARJUN SINGH): (a) to (c) A Statement is laid on the table of the Sabha. 
Statement 
(a) and (b) No Sir. However, isolated incidents have come to light from 
time to time. 
(c) Ministry of Human Resource Development and University Grants 
Commission (UGC) have issued necessary instructions in this regard to the 
Institutions of Higher and Technical Education, Education Secretaries of all State 
Governments and Union Territories. All institutions approved by the All India 
Council for Technical Education (AICTE) are required to ensure that ragging in 
any form does not take place. State Governments and educational institutions are 
also expected to exercise necessary vigil in this behalf and take preventive and 
other suitable action.

Reduction in the number of drop-out children 
†*284. SHRI RAJNITI PRASAD: Will the Minister of HUMAN 
RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) the details of the plan of Government to reduce the .number of drop-out children 
under Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan in the country; 
(b) the results achieved in this direction after implementation of the above plan; 
(c) to what extent 'Mid-day Meal' scheme has been effective in this direction; 
(d) whether any review has been made as to what extent these schemes of 
Central Government have been effective; and 
(e) if so, whether any shortcomings have been found in these schemes during 
such review and if so, the measures being taken to remove them?  
THE MINISTER OF HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT (SHRI 
ARJUN SINGH): (a) to (e) A Statement is laid on the Table of the House.  
Statement 
(a) to (e) Dropout rates have been declining steadily since launch of Sarva Shiksha 
Abhiyan. The primary stage dropout rates from 39.03% in 2001-02 to 31.36% in 2003-04. 
The dropout rate for girls declined more sharply by 11.76% points during the same 
period. 
Apart from regular monitoring by the Government of India, SSA is reviewed every 
six months by independent experts. The last review was held between 17.27 July, 2006 
which has expressed satisfaction at the remarkable progress in increasing access and 
narrowing gender and social gaps in SSA, wherein the country is fast approaching near universal 
enrolment at primary stage. The review has noted that dropout rates are declining and 
recommended that SSA needs to continue to improve retention and quality of 
instruction. 
A multi-pronged approach has been adopted under SSA for reducing dropout rates. One set 
of interventions relates to strengthening of schools and improving the quality of education 
through improvement in school

17 

RAJYA SABHA [14 August, 2006] 
infrastructure, recruitment of additional teachers, annual school grants, regular training of 
teachers, regular academic support to teachers etc. In addition, several interventions under 
SSA also aim at community support, flexible schooling for children who are dropouts, older 
children or children in difficult circumstances, and special provisions to promote education 
of girls, children from disadvantaged sections of society or children with special 
needs. 
The Mid-Day Meal (MDM) Scheme provides a hot cooked meal to nearly 12 
crore children studying at the primary stage in Government, Government aided, local 
body schools and alternative education centres. 
Reviews of MDM Scheme by the Ministry had indicated the inadequacy of 
central assistance for cooking cost and the non-availability of kitchen sheds. Both issues 
have been addressed in the revised midday meal scheme.

Steps to Increase awareness against drugs 
*283. SHRIMATI HEMA MALINI: Will the Minister of SOCIAL 
JUSTICE AND EMPOWERMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have taken any steps so far to launch drug 
awareness among the young people; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) whether it is a fact that street children and children with disabilities are 
more vulnerable; and 
(d) if so, whether Government are taking any steps to prevent such 
children from drug abuse? 
THE MINISTER OF SOCIAL JUSTICE AND EMPOWERMENT 
(SHRIMATI MEIRA KUMAR): (a) and (b ) The Government of India have 
taken the following steps to launch drug awareness among young people: 
31 

RAJYA SABHA [14 August, 2006] 
(i) Under the Scheme of Prevention of Alcoholism and Substance (Drug) Abuse, 
295 Non-Governmental Organizations were supported in 2005-2006 for 
running 31 Counselling Centres and 305 De-addiction centres. 
(ii) A National Drug Awareness Campaign has been launched on 26th June, 2006 
for drug abuse prevention among children including school going and out-
of-school youth. The secondary target audience are the parents and 
teachers. Under this campaign, the ill effects of the drugs are discussed with 
people so that correct information and life skills are available to young people 
to help them to choose a drug free and healthy life style. 
(iii) The elements of drug abuse concerns are being integrated into the school 
syllabi and curriculum by the National Council of Education Research and 
Training (NCERT). The Central Board of Secondary Education (CBSE) has 
also introduced Life Skills Education from Class VI-VIII and ill effects of drug 
abuse have been integrated into it. 
(iv) Information, Education and Communication (IEC) materials like posters, 
banners, panels, brochures, audio and visual spots have been developed to impart 
knowledge about drugs through radio, television, newspapers and other mass 
media. Special camps are organized from time to time in which the messages 
against drugs are spread through discussions, rallies, puppet shows, street 
plays and pantomime shows. 
(c) There is no specific data either for street children or disabled children. On the 
face of it, street children are more vulnerable than children living in homes. However, the 
same cannot be said for vulnerability of disabled children. 
(d) 'An Integrated Programme for Street Children' under which one of the 
components aims at reducing the incidence of drug and substance abuse among them is 
being implemented.

Performance in Basic Sciences 
*292. SHRI C. PERUMAL: Will the Minister of SCIENCE AND 
TECHNOLOGY be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that India's performance in basic sciences has come down 
in terms of percentage of contribution to world science and research; 
(b) if so, the reasons therefor and the steps taken by Government to develop 
science and technology; 
(c) whether Government have planned to set up a separate parallel mechanism for 
scientific and higher educational institutions; and 
(d) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF SCIENCE AND TECHNOLOGY (SHRI KAPIL SIBAL): 
(a) While performance of India in basic sciences, as measured by research papers published 
in cited journals, has been slowly increasing in absolute terms over the past twenty five 
years (from 14983 in 1980 to 19448 in 2005) its share as percentage of world publications 
in the basic sciences has declined from 2.9% in 1980 to 1.9% in 2005 ever, in the 
last 10 years, it has increased from 1.5% to 1.9 %. 
37 

RAJYA SABHA [14 August, 2006] 
(b) The major reason behind this phenomenon is decline of research in the 
university sector. Universities are the mainstay of research in basic sciences all over 
the world, but, in our country, univers ities have been suffering because of a 
varierty of financial and governance problems leading to, am ong other things, 
depletion of faculty and impoverishment of research infrastructure. Most 
universities fall in the domain of State Governments and they need to address 
the problems urgently. The Government of India, on its part, has taken a number of 
steps to rejuvenate and promote scientific research in universities and other scientific 
institutes of excellence. The Plan Allocation of scientific departments has been 
doubled from about Rs. 12000 crore in the IX Plan to about Rs. 25000 crore in 
the X Plan and it is planned to increase it further in the XI Plan. The Research 
Infrastructure programme of DST is a targeted programme to upgrade the 
laboratory infrastructure in universities and other higher educational 
institutions. Several institutions, centres of excellence and facilities in emerging 
and frontline areas have also been established; for example, in the areas of Brain 
Research, Marine Biotechnology, Stem Cell and Tissue Engineering, Soft 
Computing, Water Resources Development, Nanophosphors, Display 
Technology, Fuel Cell Technoloy, Ultrafast Processes, Protein Research, etc. More 
recently, two new Indian Institutes of Science Education and Research (IISERs) 
have been set up at Kolkata and Pune which, apart from carrying out frontline 
and internationally competitive research, would offer M.Sc. programmes in a multi-
disciplinary and academically flexible and research-oriented environment. 
Various agencies of Government of India have now attractive scholarship, 
fellowship and research support schemes for scientific ma npower of all ages 
starting right from the school level. 
The Government has also started some novel programmes to make our 
higher educational institutions professionally even more useful for developing 
technology. The DST programme of manpower development in collaboration with 
industry enhances the quality of technical education and makes it relevant for the 
industry through well-designed courses developed in close association with 
participating industries. A large networ k of S&T Enterpreneurship Parks and 
Technology Business Incubators has been established to synergize the technical 
expertise of engineering institutions and the commercial spirit of 
enterpreneurs for technology development and commercialization. A large 
number of technology development projects are now being jointly undertaken 
by 
38 

[14 August, 2006] RAJYA SABHA 
higher educational institutions and indu stries. All these are strong pointers 
towards improvement in indigenous capabilities for technology development. 
(c) No, Sir. 
(d) Does not arise.

RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT (SHRIMATI D. PURANDESWARI): (a) Education

to Central Board of Secondary Education, also follow a common curriculum. Schools run by 
the Central Government such as the Kendriya Vidyalayas and Navodaya Vidyalayas act 
as pace setting institutions for quality education. Under Sarva Shikksha Abhiyan (SSA), the

Inequalities in imparting education 
†1980. PROF. ALKA BALRAM KSHATRIYA: Will the Minister of HUMAN 
RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that there are a number of inequalities in the 
matter of imparting education in the country; and 
(b) if so, the efforts Government are making to remove the 
inequalities in the matter of imparting education? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HUMAN 
RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT (SHRI MD. ALI ASHRAF FATMI): (a) and (b) The 
National Policy on Education (NPE), 1986 provides for a National System of Education 
which implies that up to a given level all students irrespective of caste, creed, location or 
sex have access to education of a comparable quality. It includes a common 
educational structure, a national curriculum framework and minimum levels of learning 
for each stage of education. However, marginal difference exists in the matter of 
enrolment of girls vis-a-vis bodys at every stage i.e. primary, middle and secondary or 
SCs/STs as per the available statistics of 2003-04 collected by Ministry of Human 
Resource Development. 
† Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
82 

[14 August, 2006] RAJYA SABHA 
The NPE lays special emphasis on the removal of disparities and the equalization 
of educational opportunities by attending to the specific needs of those who have been 
denied equality so far. Concerns regarding quality and equity in education are continuously 
addressed and several measures taken which include separate schools and hostels for 
girls, exemption of tuition and other fees, incentives such as free text-books, stationery, 
uniforms, scholarships, free studentships for poor and meritorious students and 
reservations in admission. The educational development of the girl child, children of the 
weaker sections of society and the minorities is a matter of prime concern as also 
highlighted in the National Common Minimum Programme of the Government.

Elementary education as fundamental right 
1998. DR. NARAYAN SINGH MANAKLAO: W ill the Minister of 
HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that there was a constitutional amendment making 
elementary education a fundamental right, but the said amendment has so far 
not been implemented; 
(b) if so, the reasons for not fulfilling the constitutional obligation; 
(c) whether efforts are being made to create conditions to enable 
children to enjoy their right; 
(d) if so, the details thereof and by when it would be implemented; and 
(e) if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HUMAN 
RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT (SHRIMATI D. PURANDESWARI): (a) to (e) 
The Constitution (86th Amendment) Act, 2002, which came into force on 13th 
December 2002, makes free and compulsory education a Fundamental Right 
for all children in the age-group 6-14 years by inserting a new Article 21-A in part 
III ("Fundamental Right") of the Constitution. 
Based on the report of a committee set up by the reconstituted Central 
Advisory Board of Education (CABE) to suggest a draft of the legislation 
envisaged under Article 21 A, a draft Right to Education Bill 
104 

[14 August, 2006] RAJYA SABHA 
2005 was prepared and sent to all State Governments/UTs and Central Ministries for 
their views. 
In the meanwhile, the Prime Minister also constituted a small group comprising 
Minister of Human Resource Development, Finance Minister, Deputy Chairman, 
Planning Commission and Chairman of the PM's Economic Advisory Council to 
examine, inter alia, the legal, constitutional and financial implications of the Bill. 
Following the recommendations of the group and based on further consultations, a draft 
Model Bill on Right to Education, to be adopted by the States, containing provisions 
relating to the child's right to free and compulsory education of equitable quality, 
responsibility of the State and appropriate governments etc., has been circulated recently 
to the Central Ministries/Departments concerned and the State Governments for their 
comments.

Increase in power cuts 
2037. SHRI S. ANBALAGAN: Will the Minister of POWER be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the duration of power cuts has increased 
dramatically during the last three months; 
(b) if so, the State-wise details thereof and the reasons therefor; 
(c) whether the Union Government propose to chalk out any long-term 
plan to tackle the worsening power situation in the country; and 
(d) if so, the details thereof including the quantity of power production in the 
country, State-wise, and the projection, for next five years and the gap in the 
production and demand? 
THE MINISTER OF POWER (SHRI SUSHIL KUMAR SHINDE): (a) 
and (b) There has been overall shortage of power in the country during the 
current summer season except for some States. The shortages vary from State to 
State, month to month and hour to hour. The load shedding and power cuts are 
imposed by the respective distribution companies/ electricity boards depending 
on their power requirement and availability. The power demand of a State is 
met from its own generation, allocation from Central Sector Generating stations 
and through bi-lateral short-term arrangement. The main reason for short supply 
of power is increase in demand for power outstripping, the increase in 
availability of power. The details of notified power cuts during last three 
months (May-July, 2006) are given in the enclosed Statement-I (See below). 
(c) Yes, Sir. National Electricity Policy, inter-alia, envisages that 
demand of power be fully met by 2012 and that energy and peaking shortages 
be overcome with 5% spinning reserve being available. States have been 
accordingly advised to create adequate generation capacity to fully meet the 
growing demand of electricity. Central Government on its part has geared up its 
Central Sector Undertakings to enhance their generating capacity. Strengthening 
of national grid has also been planned 
141 

RAJYA SABHA [14 August, 2006] 
for providing adequate infrastructure for inter-state transfer of power to ensure optimum 
utilization of generation capacity and to transmit electricity from surplus regions to 
deficit regions. 
(d) The target for generation of power in the country is fixed on annual basis. The 
actual power generation in the country during the period April-July, 2006, and target for 
2006-07 is given at the enclosed Statement-ll (See below). 
In order to meet the objective of providing "Electricity to All by 2012", a capacity 
addition of about 1,00,000 MW is required during 10th and 11th Plan period as per 
assessment made by Central Electricity Authority. About 16,900 MW capacity has been 
commissioned in 10th Plan so far and capacity over 40,500 MW is presently under 
execution. A working group on power for formulation of 11th Plan has been set up by 
Planning Commission on whose recommendation the capacity addition programme for the 
plan would be firmed up. The power supply position would improve in the 11th Plan due 
to planned capacity addition, increase in power trading, strengthening of national grid 
for transfer of power from surplus to deficit regions and import to power from Tala 
Hydro Power Station (Bhutan).

Selection of sites for Hydro-Power Dams 
2045. SHRI S.M. LALJAN BASHA: Will the Minister of POWER be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have given any emphasis to State Government 
to go in for hydro-power generation where it entails the least Submersion of 
lands and people;

(b) if so, the details of any such guidelines given to State- Governments to 
avoid selecting sites for hydro-power plants at places involving a lot of 
displacement; 
(c) whether Government encourages dams in plain areas for power generation; 
and 
(d) the steps proposed to issue a set of guidelins on the best location of power 
plants to avoid human displacement? 
THE MINISTER OF POWER (SHRI SUSHIL KUMAR SHINDE): (a) and (b) 
Yes, Sir. As per National Electricity Policy notified by the Government in 
consultation with the State Governments, maximum emphasis would be laid on the full 
development of feasible hydro potential. As per guidelines issued by the Central Electricity 
Authority (CEA) and Central Water Commission (CWC) on preparation of Detailed 
Project Report (DPR) of Irrigation and Multipurpose Projects, the sites for setting up hydro 
power projects are selected by taking into account various factors including environmental and 
rehabilitation & resettlement (R&R) aspects. The darn height is fixed in such a way that it 
meets the hydro generation requirement and does not lead to any unnecessary 
submergence and dislocation. This aspect is examined by a number of Government 
agencies including the State Governments before taking investment decision on the

expenditure on Research and Developmen t (R&D) as a percentage of Gross 
Domestic Product (GDP) is lower compared to that in the developed countries and 
a few developing countries like Brazil and China, but it is higher compared to

various scientific and economic Ministries, income lax relief on R&D expenditure,

research establishments is the major reason for fewer students opting for science

at our scientific research establishments? 
THE MINISTER OF SCIENCE AND TECHNOLOGY (SHRI KAPIL SIBAL): (a) 
to (c) No Sir. The student's choice to take admission in various science courses is driven by 
other avenues available in the country. This is a cyclical phenomenon and is in response to

various corrective measures like enhanced research infrastructure in the universities

Disadvantages of Tribals 
2087. MISS. MABEL REBELLO: W ill the Minister of TRIBAL 
AFFAIRS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are aware of the fact that disadvantages tribals face 
in life are area specific; and 
(b) if so, the steps Government propose to take to bring about level playing field 
among the tribals themselves so that those with greater disadvantages are given 
additional support and able to make out a better living for themselves despite severe 
competition which they face among themselves? 
THE MINISTER OF TRIBAL AFF AIRS (SHRI P.R. KYNDIAH): (a) 
Yes, Sir. The Scheduled Tribes (ST) communities in the country face 
195 

RAJYA SABHA [14 August, 2006] 
disadvantages in life mainly because most of these communities inhabit areas of the 
country which are remote, hilly, undulating, forested and have tow density of 
population. 
(b) The Government is implementing a number of Central Sector/ Centrally-
Sponsored Schemes for the welfare of the Scheduled Tribes. In order to put a policy 
framework in place to provide a level playing field for the Scheduled Tribes and to 
ensure their protection and development in an integrated and holistic manner, the 
Ministry of Tribal Affairs has formulated the draft of a National Tribal Policy to 
address the issues concerning lower Human Development Indicators, poor 
infrastructure, diminishing control over natural resources, persistent threats of eviction 
from their habitat, etc. 
The Ministry has also introduced the Scheduled Tribes (Recognition of Forest 
Rights) Bill, 2005 in the Lok Sabha on 13th December, 2005, to recognise and vest 
rights over land and forest produce in forest dwelling Scheduled Tribes who have been 
residing in such forests for generations but whose rights could not be recorded.

Malnutrition deaths of tribal children in Maharashtra 
2089. SHRIMATI HEMA MALINI: Wi ll the Minister of TRIBAL 
AFFAIRS be pleased to state:

tribal children in the State of Maharashtra during the last one year; and

THE MINISTER OF TRIBAL AFFAIRS (SHRI P.R. KYNDIAH): (a) 
Malnutrition is a multi-dimensional and intergenerational problem and is not a direct 
cause of death, but it can increase morbidity and mortality by reducing the resistance to 
infections. According to the report received from Government of Maharashtra for the 
year 2005-06, the number of malnourished children in Grade III and Grade IV were

supplement nutritional deficiencies among children and pregnant women. The 
Government of Maharashtra runs specific programmes like Raj Mata Jijau Maternal 
Child Health & Nutrition Mission, Janani Suraksha Yojana and Nav Sanjtani Yojana 
which includes Mobile Medical Squad, Matritva Anudan Yojana, Dai Meeting 
Scheme, Pada Volunteer Scheme, etc. to tackle the problem.

Malnutrition in Maharashtra 
2093. SHRI SANTOSH BAGROOIA: 
SHRI GIREESH KUMAR SANGHI: 
Will the Minister of WOMEN AND CHILD DEVELOPMENT be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have taken cognizance of alarming 
increase in child mortality in the tribal  areas of Maharashtra due to serious 
malnutrition and dismal condition of the health infrastructure in these 
Districts; 
(b) whether similar situation is replicated in other parts of the country; 
(c) whether Government have made any assessment of the 
shortcomings of the anganwadis; 
(d) if so, the details and what steps are being taken to improve the material and 
human resources of anganwadis and child health care; and 
(e) if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF WOMEN AND 
CHILD DEVELOPMENT (SHRIMATI RENUKA CHOWDHURY): (a) and (b) 
As per Sample Registration System (SRS) data published by Registrar General and 
Census Commissioner of India (RGI), Infant Mortality Rate (IMR) in Maharashtra 
declined from 42 in 2003 to 36 in 2004 per thousand live birth. Similarly, the percentage 
of underweight children declined from 53.4% in 1992-93 {National Family Health 
Survey-1} to 47% 1998-99 {National Family Health Survey-2} in the Country. 
In the State of Maharashtra, prevalence of underweight children declined from 
54.2% to 49.6% during this period. District-wise data is not available either in SRS 
or NFHS. 
The work related to third National Family Health Survey is underway at present 
and results are expected to be known by the end of this year. 
(c) to (e) National Council of Applied Economic Research (NCAER) conducted 
a Rapid Facility Survey of infrastructural facilities in about 3 lakh Anganwadi 
Cantata in 2004. The report submitted by NCAER has, inter alia, brought out that. 
More than 46% anganwadis we re running from pucca buildings, 
21% from semi pucca building, 15% from kutucha building and more 
than 9% from open space. 
27% anganwadis do not have any drinking water facility. 
202 

[14August, 2006] RAJYA SABHA 
More than 45% anganwadis have no toilet and 40% have the facility of 
only urinal. 
Nearly three-fourth of Anganwadi Centres have baby weighing scales. 
Nearly 60% anganwadis have tumblers & plates. 
Right from its inception, the Scheme envisages that accommodation for Anganwadis 
will be provided by the local community. In case, however, such facility is not available, a 
room can be rented also for the purpose. However, Government has, as a special case, 
sanctioned construction of 20,000 Anganwadi Centres in North Eastern States out of the 
budget earmarked for the North-Eastern Region. Construction of 33,272 
Anganwadi buildings has also been sanctioned under the World bank assisted (COS 
Projects. The rent for Anganwadi Centres has almost been doubled recently. The States have 
been advised to provide toilet and safe drinking water facilities through convergence 
with the Accelerated Rural Water Supply/Swajaldhara Scheme and Total Sanitation 
Campaign Programme of the Department of Drinking Water Supply. For all other 
inputs, funds, as per approved norms, are being provided to the States by the Central 
Government under the Scheme. 
Out of 5652 ICDS Projects sanctioned by the end of IX plan, 763 Projects were 
in tribal areas. 
In pursuance of its commitment, as enunciated in the National Common 
Minimum Programme, the Government has sanctioned 466 ICDS Projects, including 46 
in tribal areas. These Projects are expected to become operational this year. 
For improvement of public health infrastructure, Government has launched 
National Rural Health Mission in April, 2005. 
All these measures are expected to improve the nutritional status & reduce mortality 
amongst children in the country including those of children in tribal areas.

Need for drastic changes in ICDS 
2099. SHRI EKANATH K. T HAKUR: Will the Minister of WOMEN 
AND CHILD DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the World Bank report on malnutrition among 
India's children calls for drastic reforms in the Integrated Child Development 
Services (ICDS); 
(b) whether according to the report, ICDS scheme has not been effective in 
tackling child undernutrition and it appears unlikely that the prevalence of malnutrition 
in India will fall from 54 per cent in 1990 to 27 per cent by 2015; and

undernutrition effectively?

DEVELOPMENT (SHRIMATI RENUKA CHOWDHURY): (a) to (c) The World 
Bank, in their report, titled "India's Undernourished Children —A call for Reform and

making a significant dent in child malnutrition and made certain 
recommendations to improve its effectiveness.

Family Health Survey (NFHS-II) conducted in 1998-99. NFHS-III is currently

Crimes against children 
2100. SHRI EKANATH K. THAKUR: Will the Minister of WOMEN 
AND CHILD DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that child trafficking, traditionally associated with 
only trafficking for commercial sex, is growing fast in India; 
(b) whether it is a fact that accord ing to National Human Rights 
Commission (MHRC), every y ear an average of 44, 476 children go missing 
and of these 11,008 are never traced; 
(c) whether it is a fact that there are no laws that specifically target child 
trafficking; and 
(d) if so, the steps Government propose to take to have a separate 
legislation to deal with offences against children? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF WOMEN AND 
CHILD DEVELOPMENT (SHRIMATI RENUKA CHOWDHURY): (a) and 
(b) The National Human Rights Commission (NHRC) in collaboration with 
the UNIFAM and the Institute of Social Science, New Delhi, conducted an Action 
Research on Trafficking in Women and Children in India. The study has 
brought out that child trafficking is growing in India. The Action Research has a 
chapter on 'Missing Persons and Trafficking. 'Available data shows that on a 
average 44476 children went missing every year and out of these, 11,008 
children remained untraced. 
(c) and (d) The Immoral Traffic (Prevention) Act, 1956 supplemented by the 
Indian Penal Code prohibits trafficking in human beings including children for 
purpose of prostitution and lays down severe penalties for traffickers. The 
ITPA is now being further amended providing for more stringent punishment 
for trafficking in persons including children. The

Malnourished children in India 
†2101. SHRI MANGANI LAL MANDAL: Will the Minister of WOMEN AND 
CHILD DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that out of 14.6 crores children under malnutrition all 
over the world, 5.7 crores children are in Jndia alone as per UNICEF; 
(b) whether it is a fact that malnutrition is the cause of 50 per cent infant death in 
India wherein 21 lakh infants die every year; and 
(c) if so, State-wise details thereof and the efforts Government are making in 
this regard, in this light? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF WOMEN AND CHILD 
DEVELOPMENT (SHRIMATI RENUKA CHOWDHURY): (a) As per UNICEF 
report titled "Progress for Children, A Report Card on Nutrition, No. 4, May, 2006", out 
of 14.06 crore underweight children under 5 years in the World, 5.7 crore are from India. 
However, these estimates of underweight children in India are based on findings of 
National Family Health Survey (NFHS) carried out in 1998-99. The third NFHS is currently 
underway and its finding are expected by the end of the year. 
(b) and (c) Malnutrition is a multifaceted, multi-dimensional problem and is not a 
direct but underlying cause of death as it increases morbidity and mortality by reducing 
the resistance to infections. No State Government has, however, reported infant 
deaths due to malnutrition. 
Since the problem of malnutrition is multi-sectoral, intergenerational in nature, it 
needs to be tackled through coordinated interventions in area of food security, safe drinking 
water, sanitation, nutrition, health & family welfare, poverty alleviation etc. The 
Government is already seized of the problem and a number of Schemes/Programmes are 
being implemented through various Ministries/Departments which have, direct or

food insecurity, female illiteracy, poor access to health-care, safe drinking water,

resulting in low birth weight of the new borns, poor breastfeeding and 
complementary feeding practices, ignorance about nutritional needs of infants and 
young children and repeated infections further aggravate the situation. 
The Government is seized of the problem and has undertaken several 
programmes to monitor and Improve the health and nutritional status of children.

Shri K. Natwar Singh. Member, made a personal Explanation 
SHRI K. NATWAR SINGH (Rajasthan): Mr. Chairman, Sir, when the 
situation of the people of Iraq becam e desperate, the Congress Party decided 
to send a fraternal delegation to Baghdad. The delegation was led by me. I 
visited Baghdad in January 2001. The Congress President gave me a letter of 
introduction to President of Saddam Hussain which letter I delivered to the 
Deputy Prime Minister of Iraq. Mr. Tariq Aziz, on my arrival in Baghdad. 
I made a brief call on the Oil Minister of- Iraq as a matter of courtesy 
because he had been in India and a number of other dignitaries. 
During my entire stay in Baghdad, no discussion or talk took place 
with any Iraqi authority with regard to the Oil For Food Programme, oil 
contracts, vouchers, bank  accounts, etc. The del egation was a political 
delegation. The administrative arrangem ents and the logistics were in the 
hands of Anil Mathrani, who was the Secretary of the Foreign Affairs 
department of the party of which I was Chairman. The delegation consisted of 
four members - Shri Shiv Shankar, Shri A.R. Antulay, Shri Anil Mathrani and 
me. Shri Vohra has confirmed and so has the Pathak Authority. My son 
accompanied me and I paid for his fare. There is no document approved by 
me to add any names to the delegation. I had no authority to do so. I have 
made this clear on several occasions t hat no names were added. The Pathak 
Authority has also agreed that ther e were only four members of the 
delegation. 
On my return I briefed the Congress President about our discussion 
in" Baghdad and nothing was concealed or held back. 
The Oil For Food Programme was st arted under the auspices of the 
United Nations. When complaints arose about the misuses of this programme, 
the Independent Inquiry Committee was appointed to look into these 
malpractices and abuses by the United Nations personnel in conducting this 
programme. Mr. Paul Volcker submitted hi s final report at the end of October, 
2005. The annexures to the report ment ioned my name; and the name of the 
Congress Party, as non-contractual bene ficiaries. No evidence was produced 
in the Volcker report as to how and why our names were added. I repeat, no 
evidence was produced in the Volcker report as to how and why our names 
were added.   And, by

details of Mr. Volcker's bias against those who disapproved of the U.S. actions in 
West Asia and elsewhere. My affidavit and statement to the Pathak Authority have 
been completely ignored by the Authority. 
The Permanent Mission of India at United Nations in New York, through

Concern over land acquisition under Special Economic Zones 
MS. MABEL REBELLO (Jharkhand): Sir, a mad rush to set up 
Special Economic Zones (SEZs) has begun, and this looks more like a real 
estate rush than an export rush. The Government has allowed up to 75% of 
the area of SEZs to be used for non-export purposes such as housing, 
schools, entertainment, banks and other things. 
The new policy came into force in February 2006.   But already 388 
applications  have  been  made,  of which 140  have  received clearance. 
Maharashtra has 63 applications.   Haryana, which is far away from sea, has 
53 applications. 
The Government gives 10-year tax holiday, which makes the 
corporate sector develop SEZ. SEZ is also an oasis where the industrial units 
don't have any labour and industrial dist urbance. It appears that large units 
are making SEZ units as heaven to save taxes. Some are making plans to 
shift their existing units to SEZ zone to avoid tax altogether. 
Indian companies, and funds and entrepreneurs are buying land as if 
there is no tomorrow. According to some estimates, they are in the process of 
acquiring almost 4,00,000 acres of land. 
What is the guarantee that enough export units will flock to these 
new SEZz, especially to those in St ates far away from good ports? The 
newspapers are full of stories of people wanting to set up new SEZs, but have 
very little to say about exporters wanting to rush into them. 
Government should keep a close watch on this type of land 
acquisition, lest it should contribute to  the already high cost of land and also 
lose huge revenues due to these SEZs.  Thank you.

THE MINISTER OF FINANCE (SHRI  P. CHIDAMBARAM): Sir, I 
move: 
"That the Bill to consolidate and amend the law relating to 
Government securities and its management by the Reserve Bank of 
India and for matters connected ther ewith or incidental thereto as 
passed by Lok Sabha, be taken into consideration." 
The law relating to Government Securities and their management by 
the Reserve Bank of India is laid down  in the Public Debt Act, 1944. Over the 
years, a number of rigidities and deficien cies were noticed in the Public Debt 
Act and the rules framed thereunder. The procedures provided in the Public 
Debt Act were time-consuming and some of the provisions had ceased to be 
relevant to the present context. In the wake of tremendous increase in the 
volume of public debt, the RBI, agency banks and the treasuries were 
handicapped in improving customer service. 
It was, therefore, decided to enact a new legislation in place of Public 
Debt Act, 1944, and to repeal the redunda nt Indian Securities Act, 1920, the 
predecessor Act to the PD Act. The recommendations of a Committee 
constituted to examine the entire gamut of Government securities 
management was considered for framing the new Bill. 
The Government Securities Bill was introduced in Lok Sabha on 
December 21, 2004, and referred to the Standing Committee on Finance on 
December 23, 2004. The Standing Comm ittee agreed that the enactment of 
this legislation would give greater sco pe for creation of a liquid Government 
securities market and also would bring forth considerable improvement in the 
securities transactions. 
The Standing Committee recommended five amendments and 
suggested that the Government may explore the possibility of creating a 
dedicated fund wherein unclaimed amounts of Government securities could be 
kept and accruals under which could be utilised for enabling post maturity 
interest payment in bona fide cases by amending clause 23. 
The Government examined the Report of the Standing Committee 
and accepted the recommendations of the Committee regarding the five 
amendments. On the issue of payment of post maturity interest and creation of 
a dedicated fund for the purpose, it was proposed to amend clause 23 to 
enable payment of interest beyond six- year limitation. However, it was 
proposed to delink the issue of payment of interest beyond

supported on the grounds, inter alia, (i) administrative difficulties in setting up 
28 funds; (ii) limited balances of uncla imed amounts; (iii) availability of 
payments beyond 20-year limitation for principal under extant arrangement; 
and (iv) limited anticipated inflows in future on account of demat. 
The amendments were accepted by Lok Sabha. This Bill has been 
passed by Lok Sabha with amendments. I request this House to consider and 
pass this Bill.

DR. E.M. SUDARSANA NATCHIAPPAN (Tamil Nadu): Thank you, 
Mr. Deputy Chairman, Sir. I support this Bill, the Government Securities Bill, 
2006. It is really a timely measure taken by the Government even though two 
years were lapsed after introduction of the Bill in Lok Sabha due to the 
consideration by the Standing Committee.  The aspect of giving more mobility 
to the Government securities is the nee d of the hour. Sir, the public depends 
on the Government securities rather than on shares. Even though middle class 
people have been wooed by the share market, due to the unreliability of 
shares, sensex and other things, now,  the people, especially the old-age 
people who have got their money in hand,  want to put it in the Government 
securities. They feel that it is a very secured one: That can be very easily 
transferred to their LRs in the event of their death. Making this Bill as an Act, 
Sir, is really addressing the issues of Aam-Aadmi who really need this type of 
relaxation and more flexibility in transferring the Government securities. This 
Bill provides for making the nominations when a Government security is 
purchased by a person. In this way, unnecessary litigation can be avoided and 
the LRs can very easily get that money transferred immediately or continue 
with the security in their favour. In the same way, Sir, there are more 
flexibilities provided in the case of c hanges in the securities and the loss of 
bonds. Earlier, whenever it had happened, people were having lot of difficulties 
in getting the duplicate of that particular security. Clause 11 is very much 
needed, which says, "If the person entitled to a Government security applies to 
the bank alleging that the Governme nt security has been lost, stolen or 
destroyed, or has been defaced or mutila ted, the bank may, on proof to its 
satisfaction of the loss, theft, destruc tion, defacement or mutilation of the 
Government security, and subject to such conditions and on payment of such 
fees as may be prescribed, order the i ssue of a duplicate Government security 
to the applicant." This is very impor tant. That is the need of the ordinary 
people. At the same time, I would like to draw the attention of the House to 
clause 4(2) which says: "Notwithstanding anything contained in the Benami

Need to formulate a flood control strategy 
SHRI SANTOSH BAGRODIA (Rajasthan): Sir, I rise to command the attention 
of this House to the grim flood situation in certain parts of the country. For most of 
the inundated areas, flooding is a new phenomenon that has emerged only in 
recent years, indicating a distinct change in climatic patterns. In past few years, the 
flooding has taken place within the municipal limits of towns, in addition to the 
inundating the villages. The fl ooding has revealed the strain under which urban 
infrastructure and civic amenities hav e collapsed without proper maintenance. 
Situation raises serious questions on the ability of municipal authorities in maintaining 
the drainage systems. It is a matter of concern that these regions have been flooded 
repeatedly over last few years, yet no lasting measures have been taken to 
ameliorate the situation. It has been reported that whatever measures were taken 
were inadequate and ad hoc. The local administration and police have been found 
lacking in resources and training to handle rescue, relief and rehabilitation work, 
thereby warranting the help of paramilitary and military in  work. I call upon the 
Government to 
298 

[14 August, 2006]                    RAJYA SABHA 
formulate a flood control strategy. The municipalities should be 
asked to restore the urban infr astructure and to clear the urban 
drainage system. As a part of the National Disaster Management 
Plan, the municipal staff should be trained for such exigencies. Local 
police should be given requisite training and physical resources to 
handle rescue and relief work. Instead of distributing resources as 
ex-gratia grants, investment in fl ood control should be a preferred 
option.

MR. CHAIRMAN: Hon. Members I refer with profound sorrow to the 
passing away of Prof. M.M. Agarwal, a former Member of this House on the 
14th August, 2006, at the age of 73. Bom at Chandausi in Moradabad District 
of Uttar Pradesh in April,  1934, Prof. Agarwal had his education at D.A.V. 
College, Kanpur. A teacher, an educ ationist, an economist and an 
industrialist, Prof. Agarwal participated in the freedom struggle. He was 
associated with various social welfare and educational institutions and was 
instrumental in the establishment of  several schools and colleges. Prof. 
Agarwal took keen interest in the uplift of the downtrodden, backward 
classes, minorities and other weaker secti ons of the society. He also worked 
for the welfare of women and children. He made valuable contribution in 
maintaining communal harmony among different sections of the society. A 
widely travelled person, Prof. Agarwal was Executive Chairman of the World 
Federation of United Nations, Geneva. He  also served as President of the 
Parliamentary Forum for Energy, Commerce, Industry and Social 
Development. Prof. Agarwal wrote several articles pertaining to social, 
economic, political, religious, cultural and other issues concerning population 
and family planning in various newspapers and magazines. Prof. Agarwal 
represented the State of Uttar Pradesh in this House from April, 2000 to 
April, 2006. In passing away of Prof. M.M. Agarwal, the country has lost a 
distinguished social worker, a noted educationist and an able Parliamentarian. 
I request hon. Members to rise in th eir places and observe silence for one 
minute as a mark of respect to the memory of the departed.

(a) whether it is a fact that Unit-I of Rajasthan Atomic Power Station,

(b) if so, the reasons therefor; 
(c) by when it is likely to recommence generation; 
 
(d) if not, the steps being taken by Government to copensate Rajasthan 
for loss of generation due to permanent outage of RAPS Unit-I; 
(e) whether Government of Rajasthan has requested to enhance its

(f) if so, the reasons therefor; and 
(g) the steps being taken by Government for considering the request of

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE PRIME MINISTER'S OFFICE 
(SHRI PRITHVIRAJ CHAVAN): (a) to (g) A Statement is laid on the Table 
of the House. 
Statement 
(a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) RAPS-1, first pressurised Heavy Wa ter Reactor (PHWR) set up in 
the country started operation in the year 1973. The reactor was 
designed for an economic life of 25 years. The unit has 
        been  shut down on 9.10.2004 for detailed assessment of its

Unit 1 as the detailed evaluation is still underway. 
(d) RAPS-2 (200 MWe) RAPS-3&4 (2 x 220 MWe) are in operation at

Rajasthan will also have a share of 88 MWe (20% of 440 MWe) 
from RAPP-5&6.

But, let me repeat that the original economic useful life of the unit was 25 
years. The unit has already b een operated for 31 years.  So, to say that it has 
failed is not correct. It has been shut  down deliberately. We are evaluating 
whether it will be economically feasible to run it further; and if it is found 
that it will be economically feasible, and the cost of power will be low, it will 
be run. Otherwise, it can be used as a training reactor. 
Sir, with regard to the second part of the question about the mean time 
between failures of the Indian reactors, I would like to inform the House that 
as far as Indian Pressurised Heavy Water Reactors are concerned , 14 are 
running today, entirely with our technology, four are under construction. 
These are the best operating reactors anyw here in the world. They have been 
given the awards by the Association of the Pressurised Heavy Water Reactor 
operators in the world and we are very proud of achievements of our 
scientists. They are the safest and ar e performing more efficiently than any 
other reactor in this class, working in the world.

†*307. SHRI PYARELAL KHANDELWAL:   Will the Minister of 
OVERSEAS INDIAN AFFAIRS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that death of 16 Indians in Bahrain has 
shown Government's indifferent attitude towards Indian workers working 
abroad; 
† Originsl notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
23 

RAJYA SABHA [17 August, 2006] 
(b) whether it is also a fact that the jo b of Overseas Indian Ministry is 
restricted only to overseas Indian industrialists and conferences of prominent 
persons; 
(c) if not, the details of the efforts being made by Government for the 
welfare of Indian workers working abroad; and 
(d) the details of the efforts made for the welfare of overseas 
workers by Government, with achievements, during the last three years? 
THE MINISTER OF OVERSEAS INDIAN AFFAIRS (SHRI 
VAYALAR RAVI): (a) to (d) A Statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) to (d) The Indian Embassy in Bahrain reported that on 30.07.2006, a 
major fire broke out in a two-storey building in Gudabiya, Bahrain, which 
housed about 220 Indian labourers. Sixteen Indian nationals, all from Tamil 
Nadu, died in this fire accident. Eleven  Indian nationals were injured in the 
fire and were treated in Salmania Hospital and discharged the same day. The 
fire is reported to have broken out between 0200-0300 hrs. on 30.07.2006 due 
to an electric short-circu it. One hundred and ninety-six Indian workers have 
since been shifted to another accomm odation. The Government of Bahrain 
has ordered an enquiry into  the causes that led to this fire accident and to 
verify whether the lodging provided to the Indian workers was in conformity 
with housing safety and health criteria. The Ministry of Overseas Indian 
Affairs, in co-ordination with the Indian Embassy and the Government of 
Tamil Nadu, made arrangements to se nd the bodies of the deceased to the 
respective families in Tamil Nadu. The Bahrain fire tragedy was an 
unfortunate accident in which 16 preciou s lives of Indian workers were lost. 
The Ministry has already written to the Government of Bahrain at the 
Minister's level urging grant of ex-gratia payments to the families of these 
workers who perished in the fire and to those injured. 
The Ministry of Overseas Indian Affairs was established in May, 2004 
to address the problems and concerns of overseas Indians. The Ministry's 
responsibilities include all matters relating to overseas Indians, promotion of 
investment by overseas Indians in India, interacting with the Foreign 
Investment  Promotion Board,   the Foreign   Investment 
24 

[17 August, 2006] RAJYA SABHA 
implementation Authority and other investment promotion related 
institutions. To discharge these functions, it is part of the Ministry's mandate 
to organise and participate in conferences in India and overseas. 
The Ministry, interalia, administers the Emigration Act, 1983 which 
deals with emigration of Indian citizens for overseas employment on 
contractual basis. The Protector- General of Emigrants takes measures to 
ensure the protection and welfare of th e Indian workers abroad. With effect 
from 01.02.2006, a revised and comprehensive insurance package, viz., 
Pravasi Bhartiya Bima Yojana, 2006 has been introduced which makes it 
mandatory for every emigrant  workers to have the insurance cover under this 
Scheme. Skill upgradation programmes, in collaboration with State 
Governments and other industry bodies, to enable overseas Indian workers 
seek better employment opportunities and to help them move up the wage 
chain is also an important initiative being undertaken by the Ministry. In 
addition, to ensure protection and we lfare of Indian workers abroad, a 
proposal to comprehensively amend the Emigration Act, 1983 is already 
underway. Several other measures for the benefit of Indian workers abroad 
have been undertaken by the Ministry which include streamlining of the 
emigration process through E-governance, signing of Memorandum of 
Understanding with the major labour importing countries and a publicity 
campaign to create awareness amongst potential overseas workers on their 
rights and obligations.

2104. SHRI BALAVANT ALIAS BAL APTE: 
SHRI VINAY KATIYAR:

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE PRIME MINISTER'S OFFICE 
(SHRI PRITHVIRAJ CHAVAN): (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) The Department of Atomic Ener gy has carried out research and 
development on radiation processing of food and agricultural commodities 
for the past 50 years. In 1991, the Atomic Energy (Control of Irradiation of 
Food) Rules were drafted to enable radiation preservation of food and were 
subsequently amended in 1996. In 1994, The Ministry of Health & Family 
Welfare approved radiation processing of Onion, Potato and Spices under the 
Prevention of Food Adulteration Act (PFA) 1954, Rules. The PFA Act Rules 
were subsequently amended in 1998 and 2001 in include more commodities. 
The list of commodities approved under these 
49 

RAJYA SABHA [17 August, 2006] 
Rules is given in the Statement (See below). The Department of Atomic 
Energy has set up two units for demonstration of the Technology. A 30-Ton 
Per Day capacity unit was commissioned at Vashi, Navi Mumbai, for 
Hygienisation of spices and other dry ingredients, that require relatively high 
doses of radiation. Another a 10-ton per hour capacity plant for controlling 
sprouting in stored onion and potato and disinfestations of agricultural 
commodities that require relatively low does was set up at Lasalgaon, District 
Nashik, The Plant became operational in 2003. 
(c) Yes, Sir. 
(d) Initially, the R & D work was related to understanding the effect of 
radiation on the various food and agricultural commodities later, studies were 
focused on development of preservation protocols for agricultural 
commodities like Onion, Potato, Fruits, Vegetables, Cereals, Pulses, Meat and 
Meat Product and Sea-foods. Based on these studies more than 20 
commodities (Table 1) have been approved for radiation processing under the 
PFA Act Rules. Recently, Research  and Development on minimally 
processed fruits and vegetables, ready-to-cook and ready-to-eat food products 
is being pursued. Large-scale studies involving Government agencies, private 
enterpreneurs and Non-Government Organisations (NGOs) have been carried 
out with commodities like wheat, rice, onion, potato and spices to prove the 
utility of the process. The Department has also approached the Ministry of 
Health & Family Welfare for providing generic approval to fruits, vegetables, 
cereals and pulses and their products  for the large-scale use of this 
technology. 
(e) The Department of Atomic Energy is providing the requisite know-
how and expertise for setting up Radiation Processing Plants in the country. 
More than a dozen Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) have been signed 
between Board of Radiation and Isotope Technology (BRIT) and private 
entrepreneurs for setting up Radiation Processing Plants. Under the MOU, 
BRIT undertakes to provide the radiatio n source COLBALT-60 and also the 
required engineering design and details. The Department also carries out and 
also participates in various programs conducted by other bodies, aimed at 
promoting entrepreneur development and public awareness about the 
technology.

by the Atomic Minerals Directorat e for Exploration & Research, and 
constituent unit under this Department, are 7.99 Million Tonnes. 
(b) These resources are contained in the mineral monazite associated 
with beach sand placers along the eastern and western coasts of the country as 
well as in the inland placers of Kerala , Tamil Nadu, Orissa, Andhra Pradesh, 
West Bengal and Jharkhand. 
(c) India is pursuing a three stage nuclear power generation programme 
aimed at long term energy independence based on use of our abundant 
Thorium resources. The programme is  to use Thorium for electricity 
generation in the long-term. In order to realize this goal, we are well into the 
first stage based on our modest domes tic Uranium resources. This will be 
followed by second stage comprising of fast react ors which can support a 
large power generation capacity before getting into the third stage. Thorium 
in itself can not produce electricity and it has to be first converted to 
Uranium233 in a nuclear reactor. A comprehensive three-stage nuclear power 
programme is therefore being implemented sequentially. 
(d) The third-state system (Thorium r eactors) will be deployed after a 
sizeable second stage capacity is in operation. The nuclear power generation 
during the year 2005-06 was 17324 million units (MUs) against a target to 
15560 MUs. This is based on use of Ur anium in the first stage of the three 
stage Nuclear Power Programme. 
(e) Not applicable in view of (c) and (d) above.

The employment oriented urban poverty alleviation scheme of Swarna 
Jayanti Shahari Rozgar Yojana (SJSRY), implemented by the Ministry of 
Housing and Urban Poverty Alleviation, is applicable for the all urban poor, 
living below the poverty line in urban areas, including slums. The Scheme of 
Swarna Jayanti Shahari Rozgar Yojana (SJSRY) strives for providing gainful 
employment to the urban unemployed and underemployed poor through 
encouraging the setting up of self-employment ventures by those who have 
not studied beyond 9th standard and also by providing wage employment by 
utilizing their labour for construction of socially and economically useful 
public assets. The Scheme is monitored at the National level through 
Quarterly Progress Reports received fr om the States/Union Territory (UT) 
Governments. Only State/UT-wise details  are available in the Ministry and 
city-wise data is not maintained.

AIYAR): (a) and (b) Ministry of Panchayati Raj has taken several initiatives 
ever since its inception in May, 2004 to implement Part IX of the 
Constitution in order that Panchayats emerge as self governing institutions.

constitution, composition, elections and reservations. The rest of the 
provisions are enabling provisions and involve the discretion of the State 
Governments. Hence, the first achievement of the Ministry of Panchayati Raj 
has been to build a consensus around a set of 150 points of action during

between July and December, 2004. Thes e points comprise time bound action 
plan for achieving full devolution of functions, funds and functionaries to 
Panchayati Raj Institution in accordan ce with the letter and spirit of 
Constitution. The implementation of this time-bound action plan calls for

Ministries of the Government of India dealing

(a) to (e) The State Reorganisation Ac ts of Uttar Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh

sanctioned posts, category-wise, cadre-wise and grade-wise finalized the 
distribution of posts between the su ccessor States keeping in view the 
administrative structure of the ne w successor States and their work 
requirement.

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF PLANNING 
(SHRI M.V. RAJASEKHARAN): (a) and (b) No, Sir. Under APDRP

Special Category States (all North- Eastern States, Sikkim, Uttaranchal,

Sports promotion in the country 
2257. SHRI T.R. ZELIANG: Will th e Minister of YOUTH AFFAIRS 
AND SPORTS be pleased to state: 
(a) the details of financial assistance granted by Government to 
promote sports in the country during the last three years, State-wise; 
(b) the details of the proposals formulated and likely to be 
implemented to promote sports in the country during the next three years; 
and 
(c) the necessary efforts made by Government to promote sports in the 
country? 
THE MINISTER OF YOUTH AFFAlRS AND SPORTS (SHRI MANI 
SHANKAR AIYAR): (a) to (c) 'Sports' is a State Subject under the 
Constitution and the promotion of Sports is mainly the responsibility of the 
State Governments and Sports Federations. However, the Government of 
India, directly and through schemes of the Sports Authority of India (SAI), 
augments the efforts of the State Governments and Federations in the 
promotion of sports. Financial assistance by the Government of India is not 
given State-wise but is provided against specific proposals under different 
schemes. 
The Government of India runs the following schemes to promote and 
provide incentives for Sports Activities and Sportspersons in the country: 
1. Scheme relating to Incentives for the Promotion of Sports Activities, 
which has the following components: 
(a) Sports Fund for Pension to Meritorious Sportspersons 
(b) Promotion of Sports and Games in Schools 
(c) Rural Sports Programme 
(d) Sports Scholarship Scheme 
(e) National Sports Development Fund 
 
2. National Welfare Fund of Sportspersons. 
3. Scheme of Assistance to National Sports Federations. 
4. Assistance to Promising Sportsmen under the Scheme for Talent 
Search and Training. 
212 

[17 August, 2006] RAJYA SABHA 
5. National Sports Championship for Women 
6. Scheme for State Sports Academies 
7. The Government of India also gives awards under different schemes 
to individuals and institutions. These include the Rajiv Gandhi Khel 
Ratna Awards, Arjuna Awards, Dr onacharya Awards, Dhyan Chand 
Award for Life Time Achievements in Sports and Games, Special 
Awards to Winners in International Sports Events and their Coaches 
and the Maulana Abul Kalam Azad Trophy for Universities. 
In addition, the Sports Authority of India implements the following 
sports promotion schemes in the country: - 
1. National Sports Talent Contest (NSTC) 
2. Army Boys Sports Company (ABSC) 
3. SAI Training Centre (STC) 
4. Special Area Games (SAG) Scheme. 
5. Centres of Excellence (COX). 
National and State level sports bodies 
2258. SHRI S.S. AHLUWALIA: Will the Minister of YOUTH 
AFFAIRS AND SPORTS be pleased to state: 
(a)whether Government allocate funds to support the activities of 
National and State level sports bodies; 
(b)if so, the details thereof; 
(c) whether Government representatives are deputed in the Governing 
bodies of these sports organisations; 
(d)if so, the details thereof; 
(e)if not, the reasons therefor; 
(f) whether Government are seized of the growing politicisation of 
National and State level sports bodies especially dealing with Football, 
Cricket and other popular games, and concerns of the youth, in particular, 
about the same; 
(g) whether Government are contemplating steps to depoliticise 
sports bodies; 
213 

RAJYA SABHA [17 August, 2006] 
(h) if so, the details thereof; and 
(i) if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF YOUTH AFFAIRS AND SPORTS (SHRI MANI 
SHANKAR AIYAR): (a) and (b) The de velopment of sports, including 
aspect of scouting and nurturing of talent in various sports disciplines, is 
primarily the responsibility of the State Governments and the National Sports 
Federations (NSFs) concerned. However, the Government of India 
supplements the efforts of the NSFs in various sports disciplines by providing 
financial assistance to them for purchase of equipment, scientific support and 
training by Indian and foreign coaches, holding of international and national 
tournaments in the country, sending teams abroad for training-cum-
participation in international tournaments etc. under its scheme of 'Assistance 
to NSFs'. Under this scheme, assistance is not provided to State level sports 
bodies. 
(c) and (d) There is no provision in Government guidelines to depute 
Government representatives to the Governing Bodies of the NSFs. However, 
as per the "Guidelines for recognition of NSFs", the Federations are required 
to intimate the Government well in advance about their General Body 
meetings and other meetings where the election of office bearers and other 
important decisions are to be taken and the Government has the right to send 
its observer, wherever considered necessary, for such meetings. 
(e) The National Sports Federation (NSFs) are autonomous 
registered bodies and the Government of India does not interfere in their 
day-to-day functioning. 
(f) to (i) Sports figures in the 'State List' of the Constitution and the 
Central Government does not have mandate to legislate on sports matters. 
The NSFs are registered autonomous organisations and their office 
bearers are elected as per their respective Constitutions/Memorandum 
of Associations. However, as per the 'Guidelines for Assistance to National 
Sports Federations', all NSFs are required to include prominent 
sportspersons of outstanding merit as their members on a tenure basis. 
The strength of such prominent sportspersons with voting rights should 
be a certain percentage (say 25%) of the total members representing the 
Federation.

goal that is very clear, but how to reach the end goal after having heard all 
those compelling arguments. 
Sir, I thought, first of all, I should say that over the last one-and-a-half to 
two years, this initiative, which ha s caught the attention not only of our 
country, not only of the United States, but also of countries across the world, 
is obviously a significant one. This is very clear; I don't think that we have two 
opinions on this. The initiative taken by Shri Vajpayee, through the Vajpayee-
Bush declaration, which for the first time highlighted through two lines, one 
related to cooperation in atomic energy  and the other rela ted to the Space, 
the intent to cooperate, was left to t he present Prime Minister, Dr. Manmohan 
singh, to be carried forward. So, that single line became a paragraph in 
subsequent agreements. Later on, it became texts as we advanced more and 
more into the details of this agreement. Obviously, in a area like atomic 
energy, it is never a easy walk-through; it  had to be complicated; it had to be 
intricate and that is reflected here. So, if one talks about the present situation, 
it is a natural evoluti on of these kinds of agreem ents, because these are 
unique agreements; there are no benchmarks for it. so, obviously, we have to 
accept that there could be pros and cons which one has to deal with. So, I am 
not surprised that, this kind of a nuclear deal—the Indo-US nuclear deal—has

nature and complexity of this kind of a system which can affect not only the

that it is not onl y the political parties that has debated this, the general

I don't have to say here the history of this relation with the United States in the 
area of atomic energy. In fact, it did start in a

subject like this requires a consensus backing the Prime Minister? It is 
because this is too serious a matter for the House to get divided on party lines

knew that we, as Members of Parliament, had laid down certain benchmarks 
which would reflect the consensus of t he Parliament, as a whole. Those who

predecessors in the Parliament in 1962 thought it necessary to have such a 
resolution faced with the invasion of our country by China. I am not saying that

only accepting things which we may regret later, of legislating not only for the 
present generation but even legislating for the future, if not, in perpetuity.

minimum points on which there is an agreement, lam sure, that such an 
agreement is there, but I am very sorr y to say that the Prime Minister seems 
to think that if such a resolution is passed in the House, it may be

nuclear science and technology will remain unaffected. There will be no 
external supervision of our R&D since none of the sensitive R&D facilities, 
which handle nuclear material, have been included in the Separation Plan. 
Nothing in the Separation Plan infringes on our sovereign right to conduct 
research and technology development concerning our national defence and 
energy self-sufficiency. The Government is committed to preserve the integrity 
of the three-stage nuclear power program me, including utilization of our vast 
thorium resources. Certain nuclear faci lities including Centres such as the 
Tata Institute of Fundamental Research , Variable Energy Cyclotron Centre, 
Saha Institute of Nuclear Physics, etc.  have been designated as civilian In the 
Separation Plan. As these facilities will not handle nuclear material, there is no 
question of safeguards being applied to them. We expect these Centres to 
participate as full partners in international collaboration projects.

actions to implement the cooperation could be left for discussion between the 
two Governments, the basic principles on  which such actions will rest is the

the U.S. House of Representatives. If the U.S.

Motion regarding Appointment of A Joint Committee to Examine the 
Constitutional and Legal Position relating to Office of Profit 
SECRETARY-GENERAL: Sir, I have to report to the House the 
following message received from the Lok Sabha, signed by Secretary-
General, Lok Sabha: 
375 

RAJYA SABHA [17 August, 2006] 
"i am directed to inform you that  Lok Sabha, at its sitting held on 
Thursday, the 17th August, 2006, adopted the annexed motion 
regarding appointment of a Joint Committee to examine the 
constitutional and legal position relating to Office of Profit." 
I am to request that the concurrence of Rajya Sabha in the said 
motion, and also the names of  the members of Rajya Sabha 
appointed to the Joint Committee, may be communicated to this 
House." 
MOTION 
1. That a Joint Committee of Houses to be called the Joint Committee to 
examine the constitutional and legal position relating to Office of Profit 
be constituted consisting of fifteen members, ten members from this 
House to be nominated by the Speaker including the Chairperson of 
the Joint Committee and five Members from the Rajya Sabha to be 
nominated by the Chairman, Rajya Sabha. 
2. That the terms of reference of the Joint Committee shall be: 
(i) to examine, in the context of settled interpretation of the expression 
'Office of Profit' in article 102 of the Constitution and the 
underlying constitutional principles therein, and to suggest a 
comprehensive definition of 'Office of Profit"; 
(ii) to recommend, in relation to ' Office of Profit', the evolution of 
generic and comprehens ive criteria which are just, fair and 
reasonable and can be applied to all States and Union Territories; 
(iii) to examine the feas ibility of adoption of system of law relating to 
prevention of disqualification of Members of Parliament as 
existing in the United Kingdom and considered by the Constitution 
(Forty-second Amendment) Act, 1976; and 
(iv) to examine any other matter incidental to the above." 
3. That in order to constitute a si tting of the Joint Committee, the quorum 
shall be one-third of the total number of members of the Joint 
Committee. 
4. That the joint Committee shall make a report to this House by the first 
day of the last week of the next session of Parliament. 
376 

[17 August, 2006] RAJYA SABHA 
5. That in other respects, the Rules of Procedure of this House relating to the 
Parliamentary Committees shall apply with such variations and modifications 
as the Speaker may make. 
6. That this House recommends to the Ra jya Sabha that the Rajya Sabha do join 
the said Joint Committee and communicate to this House the names of the 
Members nominated by the Chairman, Rajya Sabha to the Joint Committee." 
The above motion was adopted by Lok Sabha at its sitting held on Thursday, the 
17th August, 2006.

Review of the National TB Control Programme 
*321. SHRI S.M. LALJAN BASHA: Will the Minister of HEALTH 
AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have made some changes in the policies relating 
to the National TB Control Programme during the last six months; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) whether it is a fact that nodal TB hospitals like L.R.S. Institute of T.B. 
and Respiratory Diseases in Delhi have become noted for abandoning poor 
patients after preliminary medication; and 
(d) the steps taken to review and direct the L.R.S. Institute of T.B. and 
respiratory diseases and such other institutions to have responsible and humane 
attitude towards TB patients? 
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (DR. 
ANBUMANI RAMDOSS): (a) and (b) No changes have been made in the 
policies relating to the National T.B. Control Programme during the last six 
months. 
(c) and (d) Based on scientific evidence, domiciliary treatment was 
established as a core principle for treatment of T.B. under the National T.B. 
Control Programme since 1962. In the current Revised National Control 
Programme (RNTCP), domiciliary treatment is given to T.B. patients under 
the direct supervision of a DOT provider, in accordance with the 
internationally recommended DOTS (Directly Observed Treatment Short 
Course) Strategy. Under the RNTCP, diagnostic and treatment services have 
been decentralized to Peripheral Health Institutions (PHIs) so as to improve 
access for communities and T.B. patients. Diagnostic Centres, also known as 
Designated Microscopy Centres, have been established in the general Health 
facilities. T.B. hospitals and health facilities of other sectors. After T.B. 
diagnosis has been established, patients are referred to the treating PHIs for 
categorization for treatment and registration under DOTS. It is the 
reponsibility of the health staff to retrieve T.B. patients who default while under 
treatment and to ensure they continue DOTS treatment. Thus 
19 

RAJYA SABHA [18 August, 2006] 
under the programme, TB patients are accorded the status of a VIP and the responsibility 
of successful treatment outcome is with the health system. These patients become non 
infectious within a few weeks of starting T.B. treatment. Thus hospitalization in T.B. 
hospitals, which leads to stigmatization, is not necessary. 
However when necessary, T.B. patients can be hospitalized in general hospitals for 
other diagnostic investigations and management. Special provision has been made under 
the Programme to provide T.B. treatment in hospitals using Prolongation Pouches. 
T.B, patients after being discharged from hospitals, continue to receive DOTS 
treatment and follow up sputum examination from the respective DOTS Centres till 
they complete TB treatment and thus they are not abandoned. 
The staff at all hospitals providing T.B. treatment are given training In RNTCP in 
order to ensure high quality standardized T.B. management as per internationally 
recommended DOTS strategy throughout the country. 
All components of the Programme, including T.B. diagnosis and treatment at 
Health Units of all levels including L.R.S. Institute of T.B. and Respiratory Diseases 
and such other institutions, are monitored and supervised based on the detailed 
Programme guidelines developed for this purpose so as to ensure quality of 
services. 
The performance of the programme in all PHIs including hospitals like LRS, Delhi, 
are reviewed based on their monthly and quarterly reports and necessary feedback is 
provided.

Eradication of leprosy 
†*325.  SHRIMATI PREMA CARIAPPA: 
SHRI MOTILAL VORA: 
Will the Minister of HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether Government are making continuous efforts for eradication of 
leprosy from the country; 
(b) if so, the number of leprosy cases detected, so far, during the current 
year in the country, especially in Chhattisgarh; 
(c) the reasons for not eliminating leprosy completely from the States where 
there is much prevalence of leprosy; and 
(d) whether. Government would, with the help of concerned State 
Governments, make some special efforts for eradication of leprosy? 
THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (DR. 
AMBUMANI RAM DOSS): (A) to (d) The goal set by National Health Policy, 
2002, was elimination of leprosy as a public health problem (i.e. prevalence 
rate of less than one case per ten thousand population) at National level by 
December, 2005. The goal of leprosy elimination at the national level was 
achieved as targeted in the month of December, 2005. Elimination has been 
achieved in 26 States/UTs. Now the programme is making efforts for achieving 
elimination in remaining States/UTs, which are: Bihar, Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, 
Orissa, Uttar Pradesh, West Bengal, Chandigarh, D&N Haveli and Delhi. The 
reasons for these States/UTs not having achieved elimination are- (i) 
Launching Multi Drug Therapy (MDT) late in all the districts due to poor 
health infrastructural facilities and (ii) problem of migration of population in 
Delhi, Chandigarh and Dadra Nagar Haveli. 
Special efforts are being made in all these areas with emphasis on 
situational analysis, specific measures for case detection and treatment, 
improved supervision, giving special focus to high endemic districts and blocks 
and strong IEC efforts to promote self  referral and adherence to treatment. 
These efforts are expected to lead to elimination of Leprosy in these nine 
States/UTs. 
†Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
30 

[18 August, 2006] RAJYA SABHA 
37426 new leprosy cases have been detected so far in the country in 
2006-07 as on 30th June, 2006, out of which 1700 (4.54%) leprosy cases are 
from Chhattisgarh State. 
The Government of India is committed to implementing the National 
Leprosy Elimination Compaign throughout the country even after 
achievement of elimination at the national level. These efforts are expected to 
lead to eradication of leprosy in the long term.
